newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sony, Toshiba target global market with new PCs.
newsitem.headline: Sony, Toshiba target global market with new PCs.

text.p: Japanese computer and consumer electronics manufacturers are gearing up for global marketing of personal computers to tap the so-called "multimedia" market that combines televisions and computers.

Japanese manufacturers, fearing that powerful American PC makers may make inroads into home-use multimedia products, are trying to defend their turf by developing small, lightweight PCs that take full advantage of their expertise in miniaturisation and audio-visual technology.

Toshiba Corp, the world's top maker of notebook PCs, on Tuesday unveiled a new line of lightweight mini-notebooks and new versions of its existing notebook line-up for sale in the United States, Asia and Europe.
One new model, the 800-gram Libretto 50CT, was billed as the world's smallest and lightest Windows 95-based PC. Its list price is $1,999.

The Libretto 50CT has already been a runaway success in Japan, where it was launched in April 1996. Measuring only 22 centimetres by 1.1 centimetres, the Libretto includes a 75 megahertz Pentium processor and 16 megabytes of main memory, Toshiba said.
Toshiba, extending its reach into desktop PCs as well, also said it would start selling desktop machines for business use in Britain, Germany and France.
Toshiba plans to ship four million PCs worldwide in the year to next March 31, up 2.7 million from 1996/97.
Toshiba also started selling the Equium series of notebook PCs in the United States in March with an annual sales target of 400,000 to 500,000 units, the spokesman said.

Meanwhile, Sony Corp, boasting the top share in the global market for digital audio-visual products, announced on Tuesday that it would start selling notebook PCs in the U.S. market for the first time ever on July 1.

Sony, which abandoned the PC market in the late 1980s after its products failed to excite consumers, returned to the business in the United States in September 1996, alarmed by the possibility it would miss out in the booming market for PCs and that PCs would quickly develop into a new audio-visual product for the home.
But the company still has a long way to go to be a serious contender in the world PC market.
Earlier this year, Sony president Nobuyuki Idei said the company was still in the process of learning the PC market and he declined to reveal sales figures for the United States.

The Vaio series of notebook and desktop PCs unveiled on Tuesday feature easy-to-edit applications for motion pictures, combining Sony's audio-visual technology and Intel Corp's computer technology, a Sony spokesman said.
Sony and Intel signed an agreement to jointly develop new PCs in November 1995.
Sony will also start selling notebook and desktop PCs in the Japanese market in July for the first time in eight years, he said.
Sony said it will have monthly production capacity of 3,000 units for two models of notebook personal computers and 1,000 units for its mini-tower desktop personal computers.
Fujitsu Ltd, another Japanese electronics giant, has launched in Japan a pocket-sized computer device that allows mobile networking.

The Intertop, equipped with a color liquid crystal display and a 33.6 kilobits per second modem, offers electronic mail and facsimile functions and the exchange of data with personal computers, Fujitsu said.
